case_study_insert.main_stem: Solstice Solar Systems (SSS) is a private limited company in the renewable energy sector, installing rooftop solar panels and battery storage, with a workforce of 28. Founded in 2016 by Rohan Mehta, it operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership. SSS plans to invest $600,000 in a solar-panel assembly and battery-storage line, financed by a $300,000 five-year bank loan and a $300,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $144,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.50, and produces 36,000 units a year. SSS faces a panel rework rate of 4.1% and rising installation-quality complaints from households. Experienced installation teams set their own schedules.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: SSS assembled 36,000 solar units last year, a 9% rise on the previous year, but 4.1% needed rework and 18 warranty claims were logged last month. Only 86% of installations were completed on the booked date. A survey of 300 households found 71% would pay $0.80 more for a battery-ready system, and 47% compare installers by warranty length. Nine of the 28 technicians lack battery-storage certification; the accredited course costs $1,100 each. Panel material waste is 6.5% of purchases.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The base interest rate has risen from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing the cost of variable-rate business borrowing. (2) Lithium and solar-grade silicon input prices have risen 13.6% year-on-year, pushing up component costs. (3) The national minimum wage will rise 6.1% from $12.40 to $13.16 per hour from April 2026, raising installation wage bills.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for SSS of funding the $600,000 assembly line through a share issue rather than the $300,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Share capital does not require interest or capital repayments, so SSS keeps cash to cover $144,000 of fixed costs while the assembly line is commissioned. The base rate has risen from 4.25% to 5.0%, making the $300,000 five-year bank loan more expensive; equity avoids that interest entirely. With a $16.50 selling price and a $9.00 variable cost, each system contributes $7.50, or $270,000 at 36,000 units, and keeping that cash helps absorb the 13.6% rise in lithium and silicon prices.

Point 2: Equity is permanent capital suited to a long-lived solar and battery facility, so no lender can repossess the line if the 4.1% rework rate delays output. A share issue also spreads risk among investors instead of leaving Rohan Mehta's firm solely exposed to debt. The trade-off is some dilution of ownership, but SSS retains the $300,000 bank loan for flexibility and can use the extra headroom to improve the 86% on-time installation record.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to Solstice Solar Systems (SSS), its line investment and its cost structure.

questions.question_text: Consider national newspaper advertising, local radio sponsorship, or social-media advertising to householders. Which should SSS choose to promote its battery-ready systems? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National newspaper advertising: Newspaper campaigns could reach many householders and give SSS credibility for solar installations. However, national print space is costly for a 28-person private limited company funding a $600,000 line, and most readers are outside SSS's installation area, so the spend would be poorly targeted.

Local radio sponsorship: Radio is cheaper, reaches listeners near SSS's service area and can carry a short message about battery-ready systems. Its limit is reach and recall: with only 86% of installations completed on the booked date, a narrow local audience cannot deliver the 36,000-unit volume needed to cover $144,000 of fixed costs.

Social-media advertising: Paid social campaigns can target householders by location and interest in renewable energy, show installation photographs and measure enquiries directly. The survey of 300 households found 71% would pay $0.80 more for a battery-ready system and 47% compare installers by warranty length, both messages that can be tested cheaply online. The drawback is that online leads need quick follow-up to convert.

Recommendation: SSS should choose social-media advertising. It targets the households in the survey, is affordable alongside a $300,000 loan, and supports the $0.80 premium. National newspapers are rejected as expensive and untargeted; local radio is rejected as too narrow to fill the 36,000-unit plan. SSS should pair the campaign with prompt quoting to improve on the 86% booked-date record. SSS can measure enquiry quality against the 300-household survey before expanding the campaign.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the three promotional options with minimal application to SSS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SSS with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in the context of SSS with a justified recommendation explaining why newspapers and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for SSS of using laissez-faire leadership with its 28 installation technicians.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives experienced technicians freedom to decide how they fit solar panels and battery units on each roof. Because teams already set their own schedules, autonomy can speed up job allocation and improve the 86% of installations completed on the booked date. Technicians who control their own methods feel trusted, which supports motivation among the 28 staff while the $600,000 assembly line is being introduced.

Point 2: Technicians closest to the customer can adapt installations on site, which may reduce the 4.1% rework rate and the 18 warranty claims logged last month. Their practical ideas about battery-storage fitting suit Rohan Mehta's hands-off style, and better first-time installation protects the $16.50 selling price and the $7.50 contribution ($16.50 − $9.00). A benefit is lost if inexperienced staff lack direction, so SSS should keep clear quality checkpoints while granting autonomy. The 9% rise in systems assembled recorded in Appendix 1 makes such autonomy valuable while the new line is settling in.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual analysis linked to SSS's technicians, rework and installation record.

questions.question_text: Consider on-the-job coaching for the nine technicians or funded battery-storage certification at $1,100 each. Which should SSS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job coaching: Coaching on real installations is directly relevant to SSS's own panels and batteries, costs nothing in course fees and keeps technicians working on the 36,000-unit plan. It fits laissez-faire leadership and can be given by the most experienced fitters. However, it passes on existing habits, which may be why 4.1% of panels need rework, and it provides no externally recognised certificate for householders comparing warranties.

Funded certification: The $1,100 course gives the nine technicians formal battery-storage certification, addressing the stated skills gap and supporting the warranties that 47% of surveyed households compare. Nine courses cost $9,900 (9 × $1,100), a defined sum against the $600,000 investment. The drawback is lost installation time while staff attend, which could worsen the 86% booked-date record, and generic course content may not match SSS's exact systems.

Decision: SSS should fund the battery-storage certification for the nine technicians, followed by short on-site coaching. Certification directly fixes the gap behind the 4.1% rework rate and strengthens the warranty message to buyers, with a known cost of $9,900. On-the-job coaching is rejected as the sole answer because it preserves current habits and offers no credential; SSS can add coaching after certification to match the course to its own equipment. A further consideration is the 9% growth in systems assembled: as output rises, knowledge transfer through certification scales better than informal coaching by a few experts. SSS should also check that the $1,100 fee is covered by the $0.80 premium on enough systems before extending certification beyond the nine technicians.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two options with limited application to SSS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both options in the context of SSS.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options with a justified decision that rejects the alternative and uses the insert figures.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SSS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $144,000 ÷ ($16.50 − $9.00) = $144,000 ÷ $7.50 = 19,200 units. Answer: break-even output is 19,200 systems a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $16.50 − $9.00 = $7.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SSS's management can use this cost and break-even data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 19,200-unit break-even with actual output of 36,000 systems: the margin of safety is 16,800 units, showing how far battery-ready demand can fall before $144,000 of fixed costs is uncovered.
2. Use the $7.50 contribution to test the $0.80 premium wanted by 71% of surveyed households: the price can move above $16.50 in the model while the $9.00 variable cost is held constant.
3. Check that 36,000 units × $7.50 = $270,000 of contribution is enough to service the $300,000 bank loan as the base rate reaches 5.0%.
4. Benchmark average total cost of $13.00 a system ($144,000 ÷ 36,000 + $9.00) against the rework and 6.5% material waste to judge whether the new line is efficient.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 19,200 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 16,800-unit margin of safety against $144,000 fixed costs; $0.80 premium modelling on the $16.50 price and $9.00 variable cost; $270,000 contribution to service the $300,000 loan; unit-cost benchmarking at $13.00 to address rework and waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SSS's profitability between 2024 and 2025. Has profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.0%
ROCE 2024 = 12.0%
ROCE 2025 = 14.0%

Detailed workings: The surplus after direct costs was $396,000 − $237,600 = $158,400 in 2024 and $462,000 − $254,100 = $207,900 in 2025. Operating return on sales used $39,600 ÷ $396,000 × 100 and $55,440 ÷ $462,000 × 100. Operating return on the capital base used $39,600 ÷ $330,000 × 100 and $55,440 ÷ $396,000 × 100. Revenue rose $66,000 while direct costs rose only $16,500, so more of each sale remained after components.

Evaluation: Every measure improved. The surplus share of sales rose from 40.0% to 45.0%, which is consistent with better control of the 6.5% panel waste and a richer mix of battery-ready systems. The operating share of sales rose from 10.0% to 12.0%, showing fixed costs were spread over more output. Return on capital rose from 12.0% to 14.0% despite capital employed growing from $330,000 to $396,000, so the $600,000 assembly investment appears to be earning returns. Interest payable fell from $6,600 to $5,500, helping the operating result, although the 5.0% base rate may reverse that.

Conclusion: SSS's profitability has improved. The 40.0% to 45.0% surplus margin, 10.0% to 12.0% operating margin and 12.0% to 14.0% return on capital all point upward. The strongest evidence is the rise in return on capital, because it shows the additional capital is generating more profit rather than the improvement coming only from higher sales.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three profitability ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital movements and a justified improved judgement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SSS of charging a $0.80 premium for its battery-ready systems.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 300 households found 71% would pay $0.80 more for a battery-ready system. Adding that premium to the $16.50 price while the $9.00 variable cost is unchanged lifts contribution from $7.50 toward $8.30 a system, strengthening the cash available for the $600,000 line. It also matches the 47% of buyers who compare installers on warranty, helping SSS justify a higher-priced, certified offer.

Disadvantage: A premium is only realised if installation quality supports it. With 4.1% of panels needing rework, 18 warranty claims last month and 6.5% material waste, failures could erase the $0.80 gain through free remedial work and lost referrals. The insert gives no warranty cost, so the net effect cannot be quantified; SSS must first improve the 86% booked-date record and address the skills gap before relying on the premium. SSS should test the offer on the 300-household panel before applying it to the whole range.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to SSS's survey, quality data and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 13.6% rise in lithium and silicon input prices and the 6.1% minimum wage rise to $13.16 will affect SSS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): The rise is 0.75 percentage points. If the $300,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.0075 × $300,000 = $2,250, a manageable sum against $144,000 of fixed costs. If the loan is fixed-rate the direct effect is zero, and SSS can reduce the risk by fixing the rate. The rise also makes later finance for the $600,000 programme more expensive.

Lithium and silicon prices (up 13.6%): This attacks the $9.00 variable cost on every one of 36,000 systems. The insert does not decompose that variable cost, so only an upper bound is defensible: if all of the $9.00 rose 13.6%, that adds 0.136 × $9.00 = $1.22 a system, about $43,920 a year (36,000 × $1.22), cutting contribution from $7.50 toward $6.28. SSS can recover part through the $0.80 battery-ready premium supported by 71% of surveyed households.

Minimum wage rise (6.1%, $12.40 to $13.16 an hour): Installation wage bills rise, but the insert states neither hours worked nor technician pay, so no annual total can be invented. The defensible check is productivity: 36,000 systems ÷ 28 technicians = about 1,286 systems per technician, so the rise is affordable only if that rate is maintained or the 4.1% rework rate falls.

Conclusion: The 13.6% component-price rise will have the greatest impact. It multiplies across all 36,000 systems and directly reduces the $7.50 contribution that funds the line, unlike the conditional $2,250 interest effect and the wage rise, which cannot be quantified from the insert.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to SSS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on SSS's costs, contribution or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes using derivations shown from insert figures, with a well-justified greatest-impact judgement and reasons for rejecting the other two.
